svg.title: How Fabric Capacity Smoothing and Throttling Actually Work
svg.desc: A flow diagram: an operation is submitted and classified as interactive or background, then allowed to burst above its SKU's steady-state CU rate so it finishes quickly. The bursted cost is smoothed by spreading it across future 30-second timepoints — 5 to 64 minutes for interactive operations, 24 hours for background ones. If accumulated future usage stays under 10 minutes, nothing is throttled. Beyond that, usage escalates through three progressively worse stages: delayed interactive operations, then rejected interactive operations, then rejected background operations too, with carryforward CUs draining only when idle capacity exists at later timepoints. A warning node covers Autoscale Billing for Spark bypassing bursting and smoothing entirely, and a second warning covers Block Public Internet Access breaking Direct Lake regardless of throttling state.

text.aria-label: Autoscale Billing for Spark bypasses this entirely

svg.text: Autoscale Billing for Spark bypasses this entirely — When enabled, Spark drops bursting and smoothing for flat pay-as-you-go metering.Fabric Capacity — Bursting, Smoothing & Throttling
How CU consumption is spread over time and the four progressive enforcement stages
Smoothing (30-second timepoints) — Bursted CU cost is spread across future timepoints instead of charged all at once.SMOOTHING WINDOW — CU COST SPREAD OVER TIME (30-second timepoints)

FOUR THROTTLING STAGES (future-capacity consumed)
No throttling — Under the 10-minute overage window: operations proceed normally with no visible impact.Stage 0 — No throttling
Future usage < 10 minutes of SKU provision
Overage-protection check (10-minute window) — The decision point: is accumulated future usage under or over the 10-minute threshold?Overage protection window — all operations proceed normally.
Stage 1 — Interactive delay
Future usage 10 min → 60 min of SKU provision
Stage 2: interactive delay — Between 10 minutes and further thresholds: new interactive operations are delayed, not rejected.New interactive operations incur a 20-second submission delay.
Stage 2 — Interactive rejection
Future usage 60 min → 24 hours of SKU provision

Stage 4: background rejection too — Worst stage: background operations are rejected as well, in addition to interactive ones.Interactive ops rejected (CapacityLimitExceeded). Background may still start.
Stage 3 — Full rejection
Future usage > 24 hours of SKU provision
Stage 3: interactive rejection — Further past threshold: new interactive requests are rejected with CapacityLimitExceeded.All new requests (interactive + background) rejected. In-flight ops complete.

Key notes:

text.aria-label: Block Public Internet Access breaks Direct Lake regardless

svg.text: Block Public Internet Access breaks Direct Lake regardless — A network-isolation setting, not throttling, that silently forces Direct Lake off public endpoints. Throttling is per-capacity (not per-tenant). In-flight ops always run to completion.
Compound throttling: a chained request is throttled at most once per capacity in the chain.
Workload-specific exceptions:
Eventstreams — reduces allocated CUs rather than delaying/rejecting new streams.
Real-Time Intelligence — skips Stage 1 delay; starts throttling at Stage 2 (60-min).
Classify: interactive vs background — Fabric classifies the operation before it runs, which sets its smoothing window. Warehouse ops — classified background; benefits from 24-hour smoothing window.
SKU Quick Reference (F SKUs, F2 – F2048)
Operation submitted to capacity — Every workload draws Capacity Units from one dedicated resource pool.SKU number = capacity units (e.g. F64 = 64 CU). Each step doubles compute.
Each CU grants 2 Spark vCores × 3 burst multiplier (e.g. F64 = 384 Spark vCores).
F64+ threshold: free-license users can view Power BI content (workspace viewer role).
Bursting — The operation is allowed to consume more CUs than steady-state SKU size allows, to finish quickly.Autoscale Billing for Spark disables bursting/smoothing — pay-as-you-go mode only.
Fabric Atlas — original diagram, June 2026. Not a Microsoft asset.
